name: Keto / ketogenic diet

lead: The ketogenic diet is a high-fat, adequate-protein, very low-carbohydrate diet. It was developed as a medical therapy for refractory epilepsy, mainly in children, and is now popular for losing body fat and getting a leaner face and body. Some people also report it calming acne.

With little carbohydrate, the liver makes ketone bodies that replace glucose as fuel, and appetite often drops, so body fat falls. Wikipedia reports low-carbohydrate diets produce somewhat more short-term weight loss than low-fat diets, with the advantage fading over time, and a 2022 Cochrane review found no benefit over balanced diets at two years. Acne effects are not covered in the sources consulted.

paras: People cut most bread, pasta, sugar and starchy foods and build meals around meat, fish, eggs, dairy, oils and low-carb vegetables, often tracking carbs to stay in ketosis. Early weight changes are partly water and show within the first weeks.

Reported effects include constipation, early fatigue, raised lipids and, rarely, ketoacidosis, with case reports documented. People with diabetes, pregnancy or medical conditions are generally advised to consult a clinician first.

angle.text: Very low carbohydrate intake lowers appetite and body fat for a leaner face and body, and some users report calmer skin. Keto is an established epilepsy therapy with mixed weight loss results; acne effects were not covered in the sources here.

lead: The ketogenic (keto) diet is a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat eating pattern with moderate protein, in which the liver produces ketone bodies that serve as fuel in place of glucose.[1] It began as a medical therapy for epilepsy and became one of the most searched diets in the United States by 2020.[2] People in fitness and looksmaxxing circles use it to lose body fat and look leaner, which sharpens the face and jawline and shows more muscle definition, and some also use it hoping for clearer skin.[3][4]

Short-term trials of low-carbohydrate diets report somewhat greater weight loss than low-fat diets, with the gap narrowing over time.[3] A meta-analysis of randomized trials in overweight adults with type 2 diabetes found larger reductions in body weight and waist circumference on a ketogenic diet.[5] A 2025 randomized trial compared keto with time-restricted eating and alternate-day fasting for weight loss in adults with obesity.[6]
Within forums, keto is discussed as a cutting tool, with members posting before-and-after leanness checks and weight-loss logs, while others argue that carbohydrates matter for muscle gain.[7][4][8]
infobox: High fat, adequate protein, very low carbohydrate

paras: A classic ketogenic diet derives most calories from fat and restricts carbohydrate to a small amount so the body produces ketones. Modified versions, such as very-low-calorie ketogenic diets, are used in research on weight and conditions such as lipedema.[9] Variants discussed in lifting forums include cyclical keto, with a carbohydrate day once a week.[10]

The term ketogenic diet was coined in 1921 by Russell Wilder at the Mayo Clinic, and Mynie Peterman formulated the classic diet in the 1920s, reporting in 1925 that 60 percent of 37 children became seizure-free.[1] Use declined after phenytoin arrived in 1938 and revived in the 1990s.[1] Earlier low-carbohydrate regimens include William Banting's 1863 letter and Robert Atkins's 1972 book.[3] Keto reached mass popularity in the late 2010s, and the global ketogenic food market was valued at about 9.6 billion dollars in 2019.[2]

Proponents say cutting carbohydrate reduces appetite and water retention so they lean out faster, and some users post physique checks while on the diet.[4][8] Wikipedia reports that low-carbohydrate diets give somewhat more short-term loss than low-fat diets, around 100 kcal a day, and that calorie intake and adherence largely determine long-term results.[3] A review of the insulin and weight-loss literature discusses whether insulin sensitivity improves before or after weight loss.[11]

Reported effects include constipation, low-grade acidosis, raised blood lipids, and early lethargy that usually resolves within two weeks.[1] A review in Atherosclerosis noted rapid weight loss and favorable biomarker changes alongside a substantial rise in LDL cholesterol that makes many physicians hesitant.[12] Case reports describe ketoacidosis on low-carbohydrate diets, and headache, bad breath and cramps are common.[3]

Epilepsy trials found seizures reduced by more than 50 percent in about half of patients.[1] For weight, a meta-analysis of eight randomized trials in overweight adults with type 2 diabetes found significant reductions in weight, waist circumference, HbA1c and triglycerides.[5] The Keto-Med crossover trial compared a ketogenic with a Mediterranean-style diet on glycated hemoglobin in prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.[13] A randomized trial in women with PCOS compared moderate-carbohydrate and ketogenic diets on body measures and hormones.[14] A 2025 randomized trial tested keto against time-restricted eating and alternate-day fasting.[6] Trials focused on skin or acne were not found.

On looksmax.org, threads range from praise of keto and animal-based diets to critiques that carbohydrates are needed for muscle gain.[7] One poster shared an argument citing cardiology that LDL cholesterol is an independent risk factor, while others pushed back citing influencers who argue otherwise.[15] T Nation members describe keto as their chosen cutting method, and some use cyclical variants.[16][10] A Hacker News thread discussed large cohort studies that raised questions about low-carbohydrate diets.[17]

lore.intro: Keto is discussed on looksmax.org and T Nation mainly as a fat-loss tool, with disagreement over muscle gain and cholesterol.[7][15][16]
